s: child; offspring (person with regard to his or her parents; also a baby animal or young animal, especially as the second component in numerous compound nouns)
Er war das zweitgeborene Kind in der Familie.
He was the second-born child in the family.
Er ist das Kind zweier blinder Eltern.
He is the child of two blind parents.
Kind.et: From Middle High German kint, from Old High German kind, from Proto-West Germanic *kind, from Proto-Germanic *kindą, *kinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth”).

s: nursery school; kindergarten; day care center (institution where children below school age play and are looked after during the day)
antics, petty squabbling (behavior considered undignified and unproductive, often antagonistic and cliquish)

_Du_ hast aber schon gemerkt, dass [...] nicht von mir war, ja?
*kopfschüttel* So ein Kindergarten, hier.

_You_ did notice that [linked message] wasn't written by me, didn't you?
*shakes head* Some schoolyard-level discussion, this.
Kindergarten.et: Kind (“child”) + -er- + Garten (“garden”). Coined by German pedagogue Friedrich Fröbel in 1840 in the metaphorical sense of "place where children can grow in a natural way", not in the literal sense of "garden".

s: a kind of Fleischwurst sausage from finely ground meat scraps which is similar to mortadella without the fat cubes; contains a high amount of gelatin to give a soft, moist texture that makes it appealing to children.
Na, Kleiner, willst du eine Scheibe Kinderwurst?
Hey, little man, you want a piece of bologna?
good upbringing, particularly good manners or education
paediatrician (UK), pediatrician (US) (male or of unspecified gender)
Official/institutionalized hostility or coldness towards children; kinderfeindlichkeit.

Kino.et: Clipping of Kinematograph m. Originally also used a masculine noun (der Kino).

Kinn.et:
From Middle High German kinne, from Old High German kinni, from Proto-West Germanic *kinnu, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu-, *ǵénus (“chin, jaw, cheek”).
Compare Low German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin, Danish kind, Icelandic kinn…

s: the portion of the beard on the chin, especially (but not exclusively) when trimmed in the form of a goatee
day care center; nursery school; kindergarten (for preschool children)
Viele kinderlose Frauen sprechen öffentlich über ihre Sehnsucht nach einer Familie. Der Therapeut Matthias Stiehler weiß, wie es kinderlosen Männern gehen kann. Und was ihnen bei der Sinnfrage hilft.
Many childless women speak publicly about their longing for a family. Therapist Matthias Stiehler knows what the experiences of childless men can be like. And what helps them find purpose.

Kindheit.et: From Middle High German kintheit, from Old High German kindheit (also kindesheit), equivalent to Kind + -heit.

s: baptism; the ceremony of consuming beer to mark a baptism
Kindelbier.et: A compound of Kindel, an Upper German dialectal diminutive of Kind, and Bier.

s: a carriage for a baby or small child, especially a pram/baby carriage, but also a pushchair/stroller
"children, kitchen, church"; the traditional woman's realm
cot death, crib death, sudden infant death syndrome (unexplained death of a baby, usually while sleeping)

kindlich.et: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]; Kind (“child”) + -lich.

s: nanny (female) (cf. männliches Kindermädchen (“male nanny or manny”))
child benefit (state payment to people with children)
child molester, child abuser (one who performs sexual acts on a minor)
child's bicycle (a bicycle adapted for children's necessities)
wish or desire to have children
plantlet (a young or small plant used as a propagule)
Kindel.et: Inherited from Middle High German kindel, from Old High German chindili. By surface analysis, Kind + -el.

s: kindergarten teacher, kindergartner (kindergartener) (male or of unspecified gender)
out of the mouths of babes comes truth: children have a pure heart and an original intuition, which makes them wise
out of the mouths of babes comes truth: children have no social inhibition and therefore speak their mind
Kindermund tut Wahrheit kund.et: Literally, “child's mouth makes the truth known”.

s: Ach! laßt mich reden! laßt mir meine Narrenfreiheit! Ich sage ja nichts anderes, als was unsere Kindeskinder sagen werden.
kindergarten teacher that has completed a degree in early childhood education
academic in the early childhood education field

The organized rescue of (predominantly Jewish) children from Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and the Free City of Danzig, placing them in British foster homes, shortly before the outbreak of the Second World War.
1912, Martin Luther, Lutherbibel von 1912, Jeremiah 4:31 (with KJV translation)

For I have heard a voice as of a woman in travail, and the anguish as of her that bringeth forth her first child, the voice of the daughter of Zion, that bewaileth herself, that spreadeth her hands, saying, Woe is me now! for my soul is wearied because of murderers.
A kitchen knife specifically designed to be used by children

Kindermord.et: From Kind + -er- + Mord. Cognate with Dutch kindermoord.

s: children’s well-being (preservation of the physical and mental integrity and sufficient support (for the development) of a child)
In Deutschland darf der Vorname dem Kindeswohl nicht schaden, indem er das Kind lächerlich machen oder eine Verbindung „zum Bösen“ herstellen würde, wie durch die Namensgebung Judas oder Kain.
In Germany, the first name must not harm the children’s well-being by ridiculing the child or making a connection “to evil”, as by naming it Judas or Cain.
to invite friends and relatives for drinks after childbirth (a traditional obligation of the father still upheld in rural parts of Northern Germany, including the Münsterland)
evacuation of children in Germany during World War II
pediatrics (branch of medicine that deals with the treatment of children)
a name in older literature for Hadza, of unknown but presumably Bantu origin. Presumably cognate with Tindiga.
Stupsnase, rundliche Wangen und große Augen – ein Baby! Kaum ein Erwachsener ist gegen das Kindchenschema immun, es erweicht das härteste Herz und löst Beschützerinstinkte aus.
Kindchenschema.et: Coined by Konrad Lorenz in 1943, Kindchen + Schema.

s: car seat (detachable seat for young children)
Zur Belohnung dafür, dass die Herrn Fabrikanten alle während der letzten 22 Jahre erlassnen Gesetze über Kinderarbeit aufs frechste ignorirt hatten, ward ihnen jetzt aber auch die Pille vergoldet.
A small cutlet, suitable for a child to eat.
with many children, with multiple children
Children's Crusade (episode of popular crusading in 1212, traditionally misunderstood as mainly perpetrated by children)
Schnee fiel, als man sich's erzählte / In einer östlichen Stadt / Von einem Kinderkreuzzug / Der in Polen begonnen hat.
Ihr moralischer Eifer, die sektenhafte Gewissheit, die humorfreie Klarheit, für die richtige Sache zu kämpfen, wirken wie ein hipper Öko-Kinderkreuzzug.
Kinderkreuzzug.et: Kind + -er- + Kreuzzug, calque of Latin peregrīnātiō puerōrum.

s: child rapist: a person who rapes child(ren)
children's book author, writer of children's books
knick-knacks; odds and ends (things of little value; especially worthless jewellery)
Auf den ersten Blick sieht man sie kaum. Auf den zweiten auch nicht. Junge Männer und Frauen, die gegen den Klimawandel, gegen Krieg und andere Kinkerlitzchen demonstrieren.
silliness; frivolity; foolishness (that which is absurd or a waste of time)
Oft, besonders in jungen Jahren, meinte er wohl, es sei doch besser, was Rechtes zu lernen und ein nützlicher Bürger zu sein, als solche Kinkerlitzchen zu machen.
Kinkerlitzchen.et: Kinkerlitz m + -chen, from French quincaille(rie) (“metal hardware”) + -chen (diminutive suffix), originally in reference to worthless jewellery.

s: nursery rhyme (short poem or song for children, mostly anonymous or handed down by folklore)
Es folgen ein europäischer Haftbefehl, die Festnahme am Hamburger Flughafen und eine Fahrt im Gefängnisbus bis nach Österreich. Dort muss der einstige Kinderstar jetzt auf den Gerichtsprozess warten.
childhood dream, wish or desire held since a young age
only used in von Kindesbeinen an

Kinder, die was wollen, kriegen was auf.i: /ˈkɪndɐ ˌdiː vas ˈvɔlən ˈkʁiːɡən vas ˌaʊ̯f di ˈbɔlən/
s: a phrase used to teach children that they should say ich möchte or ich hätte gern (“I’d like”) instead of ich will (“I want”)
„Mama, ich will ein Eis!“ – „Kinder, die was wollen, kriegen was auf die Bollen!“
Kinder, die was wollen, kriegen was auf.et:
Literally, “children who want something get something on their thighs / buttocks”.
Probably a calque from Low German. The anatomical use of Bollen is especially Westphalian, where the phrase is attested in 1912 as Kinner, die wat wollen, kriegt wat op den Boll…
